messages.subject: Model with data augmentation
parts:
Dear team, 
I hope this email finds you well. 
I have been using a multi-state model to estimate population sizes and transition probabilities as presented in the BPA book.
I am working on a simulated population, right now and I am having quite an interesting behavior in my model.
I have run the model several times (more than 50) to check how reliable are the estimates and half of the time the model wants to use all the data augmentation given to it, so the first or second estimates or population size are considerable high (almost the size of the date set with the augmented data) and then it suddenly gets super close to the simulated sample size. sometimes it stats well and the jump is in the middle or at the end.
has someone experienced similar behavior? if so, how is it possible to handle it?

Thank you in advance :)

When this matrix is constant (the input is an exact probability) the problema seems to be solved, once you start giving more flexibility to the model (changing the exact value to a distribution such as uniform or beta) the jump start to appear. The narrower the distribution, the less common it is. 

I would appreciate any idea or comments, I had try several distributions, lengths of chains, blocking parameters, slice sampling... And the problem seems to persist.

Thank you for your time :)

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: Re: Model with data augmentation
parts:
Dear Diego,

perhaps that scale prior of Link may be useful for you. When doing data augmentation, you augment the detection histories with all-zero histories and then add another hierarchical level to your model which decides whether an individual is 'real' or not. This model for the data augmentation variables is a Bernoulli with some success probability, omega say. The usual choice for a prior for omega is a uniform, which is then equivalent to putting a discrete uniform prior on population size N. However, Link shows that this choice sometimes makes the estimate of N to "run away", and that this can be prevented by that scale prior.

Not completely sure this is the solution, but I just wanted to follow up.

best regards  -- Marc

# Likelihood
for (i in 1:M){

# Observation process

y[i,1] ~ dbern(mu1[i])

On Wed, 14 Sep 2022 at 17:55, Marc Kery <marc...@vogelwarte.ch> wrote:
Dear Diego,

perhaps that scale prior of Link may be useful for you. When doing data augmentation, you augment the detection histories with all-zero histories and then add another hierarchical level to your model which decides whether an individual is 'real' or not. This model for the data augmentation variables is a Bernoulli with some success probability, omega say. The usual choice for a prior for omega is a uniform, which is then equivalent to putting a discrete uniform prior on population size N. However, Link shows that this choice sometimes makes the estimate of N to "run away", and that this can be prevented by that scale prior.

Not completely sure this is the solution, but I just wanted to follow up.

best regards  -- Marc
